newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thousands mourns Hong Kong islands activist.
newsitem.headline: Thousands mourns Hong Kong islands activist.

text.p: Thousands of mourners paid a last tribute on Sunday to David Chan, the activist who died in a protest over Japan's control of a chain of islands in the East China sea.
Chan, a 45-year-old media consultant, drowned on September 26 after jumping from a ship into waters near the islands.

The activist was mourned as a hero as his gold-trimmed black coffin was wrapped in the Chinese communist red flag before being taken to a crematorium in east Hong Kong island. The body was later cremated.
A friend and commrade-in-arms, Mak Wah-chueng, said in a memorial speech, "We will always remember you."
The mourning hall, bedecked with yellow silk and white chrysanthemums and crammed with banners and wreaths reading "Noble spirit live forever," was jammed with people.
They included Hong Kong government officials, Chinese envoys, fellow activists, prominent politicans and businessmen, who burned sticks and bowed to an altar bearing a picture of Chan.
Chan's wife also burned joss sticks in tribute.
The activist's family said they had asked the Chinese government to help them to have his ashes scattered on the disputed islands.
In the meantime, they would keep the ashes in a Buddhist temple in the rural New Territories of Hong Kong.
Some supporters waiting outside the funeral home clapped in respect for Chan as the hearse left for the crematorium.
Chan was the first casualty in two months of protests.
Anti-Japanese sentiment flared after Japanese extremists erected a lighthouse and flags on the islands, which Japan calls the Senkakus and which China claims as the Diaoyu isles.
Japan has claimed the potentially resource-rich islands, since 1895 and refuses to admit that their sovereignty is open to discussion. China has claimed them for centuries.
